slides.title: Chapter 9: Transaction Fees
slides.sub: Who pays a fee, how it is priced, replaced and bumped, and what moved since print

items.body: Python 3.14.6 on the chapter's own library; Bitcoin Core 31.1 results are recorded from one test run, not run here.

slides.notes: This deck explains transaction fees: who pays them, how they are priced, how a payment is replaced or bumped, and what changed since the book went to print. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library. Bitcoin Core 31.1 was run once on a test network, and its answers are only read back, so they are labelled as recorded. The course page for chapter 9 carries the full text, the sources and the code that runs.

slides.title: Today's route through seven parts
slides.sub: Seven parts; every number is a slide you can jump to

items.label: code examples with a picture of each result

slides.notes: The route has seven parts that follow the order of the chapter. Four true stories and twenty-seven code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing in this deck can be run and edited there. Each part opens with a divider that states, in one line, what the part establishes, and closes with the example that proves it.
slides.take: Seven parts, twenty-seven examples, four true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

items: Who pays a transaction fee, and why is it not a field of the transaction?
How is a fee rate computed, and which minimum rates apply?
How does a node estimate a fee, and what do two real blocks show?
What must a replacement pay, and why is full replacement now the default?
How does a child pay for its parent, and what does package relay add?
How can a family pin a payment, and what do TRUC and anchors change?
What is fee sniping, and why do wallets lock a payment to the tip?

slides.notes: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide of this deck. They cover who pays a fee, how a fee rate is computed, how a node estimates a rate, what a replacement must pay, how a child pays for its parent, how a family can pin a payment, and what fee sniping is. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter, and the summary returns to them.

slides.title: Who pays the fee
slides.sub: The spender pays the fee: it is the part of the inputs that no output claims.

items.meaning: The fee is inputs minus outputs; no field holds it.
Only the spender can add to the fee, since the signature covers the amounts.
Miners choose what goes into a block and prefer the highest rates.

slides.notes: A transaction has no fee field. The fee is what the inputs hold and the outputs do not claim, so the spender pays it and only the spender can change it. This part shows how to see that in the raw bytes, what goes wrong when the change output is forgotten, and why nobody else can add to the fee of a signed payment. The three examples of the part are computed from one recorded run of Bitcoin Core.

slides.title: What a forgotten change output costs
slides.sub: A 20 coin input, a 1 coin output and no change output

groups.note: A payment spends 20 coins, sends 1 and forgets its change.
The node's error text names the safety limit maxfeerate.
Mined with the limit lifted, the miner gets subsidy plus fee.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: the miner's reward, satoshis
The node said max-fee-exceeded. With the limit lifted, the reward 4,400,000,000 equals subsidy plus fee: yes.

slides.notes: If a wallet forgets the change output, the difference between inputs and outputs becomes an enormous fee. The node refuses the payment with the reason max-fee-exceeded, which is a safety limit and not a consensus rule. Mined with that limit lifted, the miner's reward equals the subsidy plus the fee, which shows where the money went. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A safety limit protects the spender from paying nearly everything as fee

slides.title: Only the spender can raise the fee
slides.sub: Editing an amount after signing

groups.note: One payment as signed, and a copy with its output cut.
The node rejects the copy: the signature covers the amounts.
The cut is the extra fee; only the spender could add it.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: the same payment, signed and edited
The cut of 5,000 satoshis breaks the signature: mempool-script-verify-flag-failed.

slides.notes: The listing cuts the first output of a signed payment by 5,000 satoshis. The node rejects the copy because the signature covers the amounts and no longer fits. So the fee belongs to the spender: anyone else who wants a payment confirmed sooner must pay in a second transaction, which is the idea of child pays for parent in a later part. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The signature covers the amounts, so nobody else can add to the fee

slides.title: Fees and fee rates
slides.sub: A fee is a sum in satoshis, and the fee rate is that sum per unit of virtual size.

items.meaning: Virtual size is the space a payment takes in a block.
A rate is the fee over the virtual size, in satoshis per byte.
Nodes, wallets and dust rules each set a floor.

slides.notes: Miners are paid by the space a payment takes, not by its value. This part measures size, weight and virtual size, turns a fee into a rate, and meets the floors that nodes, wallets and dust rules set. Block space is limited, so the fee rate is the unit in which payments compete. The five examples of the part measure one payment, one block and three kinds of minimum.

slides.title: Size, weight and virtual size
slides.sub: Three measures of one payment

groups.note: One payment of the test node, parsed from its hex text.
Witness bytes count a quarter, so weight is not size.
Virtual size is weight over four, rounded up.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: four measures of one payment
Virtual size 141 is the weight 561 over four, rounded up: the ratio is 0.2513.

slides.notes: One payment has 113 bytes without witness data and 222 bytes in all. Its weight is 561 units, because witness bytes count one each and the other bytes four. Its virtual size is 141, the weight over four rounded up. Fees and block space are measured in this unit, so two payments with the same value can differ in cost. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Fees are charged per virtual byte, which is the weight over four

slides.title: A fee rate and its units
slides.sub: Satoshis per virtual byte, or coins per thousand bytes

groups.note: The rate is the fee divided by the virtual size.
Coins per thousand bytes convert to satoshis per byte.
Two spellings of one rate give one fee: mind the units.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: rates and their units
A coin-per-kilobyte rate is a hundred thousand times smaller as a number than the same rate in satoshis per byte.

slides.notes: The rate is the fee over the virtual size: 282 satoshis over 141 virtual bytes gives 2 satoshis per byte. Some tools speak in coins per thousand bytes, so 0.0000657 means 6.57 satoshis per byte. Two spellings of ten satoshis per byte give the same fee, and a wrong factor gives an absurd one, which is why the units must always be written next to the number. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Mixing the units changes the fee by a factor of a hundred thousand

slides.title: Space in a block is limited
slides.sub: The block weight limit and a real block

groups.note: The limit is a consensus constant in the saved source.
Block 840,000 weighs almost exactly as much as the limit.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: weight units of a block
The block fills 99.83 percent of the 4,000,000 units, so payments compete for room.

slides.notes: The consensus limit is four million units of weight per block. Block 840,000 weighs 3,993,281 units, which is 99.83 percent of the limit. When blocks are full, payments must bid for room, and the fee rate is the bid. The limit is a constant in the saved source of Bitcoin Core, so the listing reads it from there instead of typing it. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A full block makes fee rates compete

slides.title: The minimum relay fee
slides.sub: Why 14 satoshis were not enough for 141 bytes

groups.note: Three payments of 141 bytes, paying 8, 14 and 15 satoshis.
Only the last is taken; the node's floor is 0.1 per byte.
141 bytes at that floor cost 14.1, so 15 is the least.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: three fees for 141 virtual bytes
At 0.1 satoshi per byte, 141 bytes cost 14.1 satoshis: 15 is the smallest whole fee.

slides.notes: A node relays only payments above its floor, here a tenth of a satoshi per byte. For 141 bytes that is 14.1 satoshis, so payments of 8 and 14 satoshis are refused and one of 15 is accepted. The floor protects nodes from spam, and it is policy, not consensus: another node may set it differently. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A fee below the floor is not relayed, however valid the payment

slides.title: Dust and the wallet's floor
slides.sub: Outputs too small to be worth spending

rows: wal = ['ok' in w[k] for k in ks]
groups.note: The wallet refuses 0.5 and 0.1 satoshis per byte, takes 1.

rows: dust = {k: (n + 67) * 3 for k, n in sz.items()}
groups.note: Dust costs more to spend than it holds: (size + 67) x 3.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: dust limit of three output types, satoshis
The wallet refused 0.5 and 0.1 satoshis per byte and took 1: refused, refused, accepted.

slides.notes: An output is dust when spending it would cost more than it holds. The limit is three satoshis for each byte of the output plus its spending input, which gives 294 satoshis for the common segwit key output. The anchor output is the smallest limit of the three. The wallet in this run also refuses rates below one satoshi per byte. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Wallets keep stricter floors than nodes; dust is a floor on outputs

slides.title: Fee estimation from past blocks
slides.sub: Estimating a fee means reading past blocks to find the rate that confirmed in time.

items.meaning: The estimator reads recent blocks to answer for a target.
Two real blocks show how far fee rates can move.

slides.notes: A wallet must guess a rate that will confirm in time. This part shows how the estimator learns from past blocks, where its answers stop, and how two real blocks show a market that moves by a factor of five hundred. An estimate is a summary of what earlier blocks confirmed, so it can only be as good as the history it has seen. The three examples of the part use one recorded run and the census of two mainnet blocks.

slides.title: Two blocks, two fee markets
slides.sub: The median fee rate of the highest-paying payments

groups.note: The census holds the 599 best-paying payments of two blocks.
The median fee rate fell from over a thousand to three.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: median fee rate, sat per byte
Among the 599 highest-paying payments of each block, the median rate fell from 1,436.45 to 3.02.

slides.title: Replace by fee (RBF)
slides.sub: Replacing a payment means sending a conflicting copy that pays a higher fee.

items.meaning: A sequence number says whether replacement is welcome.
A new copy must pay more than the old one, by a step.
Replacements can pay a payee twice or be cycled to cause harm.

slides.notes: A payment that waits too long can be replaced by a copy that pays more. This part runs the signal that invites replacement, the rules a replacement must meet, the default that changed in release 28.0, and the hazards of replacing. The rules are policy, so they changed with releases of Bitcoin Core. The four examples of the part replace payments on a test network.

slides.title: The opt-in replacement signal
slides.sub: BIP 125: a sequence number that invites replacement

groups.note: A low enough input sequence number signals replaceability.
Most payments of the halving block signal; fewer later.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: the signal and its use
One low sequence number is enough to signal, and fewer payments signal in the later block.

slides.notes: A payment signals that it may be replaced when one of its inputs has a sequence number below 0xfffffffe. In the halving block 485 of 599 payments signalled; in block 971,489 only 273. The signal matters less now that replacement needs no signal, but it still tells other software what the sender intends. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.

slides.title: A replacement must pay enough
slides.sub: Four conflicting copies of one 564-satoshi payment

groups.note: A payment of 564 satoshis meets four conflicting copies.

rows: taken = ['ok' in X[k]['result'] for k in ks]
groups.note: Each copy has its own fee; the node accepts or refuses.
Rule: old fee plus new size at the incremental rate.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: four copies of a 564-satoshi payment
The old fee plus the new size at the incremental rate: 579 pass, 578 do not.

slides.notes: A replacement must pay more than the payment it replaces, and it must also pay for its own size at the incremental rate. For a payment of 564 satoshis and 141 bytes the least acceptable fee is 579. The copies at 514, 564 and 578 are refused, and the one at 579 is accepted. The listing sends four conflicting copies of one payment to the node and records whether each is accepted. It is example 13 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Pay the old fee plus the new size at the incremental rate

slides.title: Full replacement is the default
slides.sub: A payment that never signalled is replaced

groups.note: The first payment has a final sequence: it never signalled.
Yet a conflicting payment replaced it: full replacement is on.
The switch to turn that off was removed in 29.0.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: a payment that never signalled
A payment without a signal was replaced, and the switch that turned this off is gone.

slides.notes: The first payment used the final sequence number, so it never asked to be replaceable. A conflicting payment replaced it anyway. Release 28.0 made full replacement the default and release 29.0 removed the option, so starting the node with it off now fails. The book describes the older rule, so this is a change since print. It is example 14 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Bitcoin Core 31.1 replaces without a signal and has no switch to stop it

slides.title: A node that only listens to replacements
slides.sub: Peter Todd's build, 12 December 2022

items.cap: Accepted Here sign - ninjarobot, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

items: On Monday 12 December 2022 Peter Todd posted to the bitcoin-dev list a build of Bitcoin Core 24.0.1 carrying Antoine Riard's full-rbf peering code.
Release 24.0.1 had just added mempoolfullrbf, off by default, so only transactions that opted in could be replaced by another payer.
Todd's build advertises a FULL_RBF service bit and peers with others doing the same, so replacements travel reliably across roughly thirty nodes.
Bitcoin Core 28.0 made full replacement the default in 2023, and 29.0 removed the option entirely.

items.body: Stand-in picture: an accepted-here sign, not the post

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 12 December 2022. Peter Todd posted to the bitcoin-dev list a build of Bitcoin Core 24.0.1 that carries Antoine Riard's full-rbf peering code, so that nodes willing to replace could find each other. The lesson is that policy is what most nodes choose to relay, and it changes by their choice. The picture is a stand-in; the link leads to the post.

slides.title: Paying the payee twice
slides.sub: Three versions of one payment

groups.note: Three versions of one payment, each replacing the last.
Versions 0 and 1 conflict, 1 and 2 conflict, 0 and 2 do not.
So 0 and 2 can both be mined: the payee is paid twice.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: payee's amount, satoshis
Versions 0 and 2 do not conflict (no): both were mined and the payee got double.

slides.notes: Three versions of a payment replace each other in turn. Versions 0 and 2 do not conflict, so once version 0 is mined, version 2 can be mined as well. The payee asked for 40,000,000 satoshis and received 80,000,000, so the sender pays twice. This is a hazard of replacement for the sender for the payee. It is example 15 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Replacing is not undoing: an old version may still be mined

slides.title: Is a rule policy or consensus?
slides.sub: Why a payment can be valid and still not be relayed

left.head: Consensus decides what is valid
rows: Every node must agree, or the chain splits.
The block weight limit is one such rule.
A change needs a soft or hard fork.

right.head: Policy decides what is relayed
rows: Each node may choose its own rules.
Relay floor, replacement rules, TRUC and cluster limits are policy.
A change needs only a new release.

slides.notes: Most rules of this chapter are policy: the relay floor, the replacement rules, the version 3 limits and the cluster limits. A payment that breaks them can still be valid in a block that a miner builds. Policy changes with a release of the software, which each node operator may or may not install; consensus changes only by a fork, which every node must follow. The block weight limit is the one consensus rule of the part.
slides.take: Policy can change with a release; consensus changes only by a fork

slides.title: Child pays for parent (CPFP)
slides.sub: A child spends the parent's output and pays a fee large enough for both.

items.meaning: Miners price a parent and its child together.
Nodes accept a pair that a single payment could not be.
Connected payments are grouped and ordered as one cluster.

slides.notes: When the parent cannot be changed, a child can pay for it. This part measures the package rate, shows why nodes now relay packages, and meets the cluster mempool that replaced the old chain limits. A child spends an output of the parent and pays a fee large enough for both, so miners take the pair together. The five examples of the part run on a test network of Bitcoin Core.

slides.title: Child pays for parent (CPFP): key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: a concept of the chapter and its meaning

items.label: Child Pays for Parent (CPFP) Fee Bumping
items.meaning: A child spends the parent's output and pays enough for both. Also written: CPFP (child pays for parent) fee bumping.

Miners treat the pair as one package of 50.77 satoshis per byte, which beats a waiting payment at 20, so the pair is mined first. slides.title: Cluster limits of the mempool
slides.sub: The cluster mempool of Bitcoin Core 31

groups.note: The mempool groups connected payments into clusters with limits.
A chain of 65: 64 accepted, the next one refused.
The old 25-ancestor limit is gone: a chain of 26 passes.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: limits on one cluster
Size is limited per cluster; the old limit of 25 ancestors no longer applies.

slides.notes: Release 31.0 groups connected payments into clusters, limited to 64 payments and 101,000 virtual bytes. Of a chain of 65, 64 are accepted and the next is refused as a too-large cluster. The old limit of 25 ancestors is gone, so a chain of 26 is accepted. The limits are policy and can change again. It is example 19 in the chapter code tab of the course page.

slides.title: Pinning, anchors and fee bumping
slides.sub: Pinning makes a parent hard to replace; an anchor output keeps a fee bump possible.

items.meaning: One extra small child was allowed beyond the usual limits.
Version 3 payments get strict limits that bound pinning.
A small output lets any party add a fee later.

slides.notes: A large child can make a parent costly to replace, and a pre-signed payment cannot guess a future fee. This part runs the carve-out, the version 3 limits and the pay-to-anchor output that answer both problems. Each of them is policy that was added to keep a fee bump possible when the fee is not known in advance. The four examples of the part are followed by the story of the carve-out.

slides.title: A big child pins its parent
slides.sub: Replacing a parent costs more when its child is large

groups.note: A parent paying 705 satoshis gets a child of 90,012 bytes or 885.
To replace the parent, pay for the whole pinned family.
A capped version 3 child cuts the price about 88-fold.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: cost to replace the parent, satoshis
The parent pays 705. A pinned family of 90,012 bytes costs 450,780 to replace; a capped one only 5,145.

slides.notes: A parent that pays 705 satoshis gets a child of 90,012 bytes. To replace the parent, the replacer must pay for the whole family: 450,780 satoshis. With a version 3 child, capped at 1,000 bytes, the same replacement costs 5,145 satoshis, about 88 times less. That is why the cap bounds pinning. It is example 21 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Cap the size of the child and pinning becomes cheap to undo

slides.title: TRUC limits on a family
slides.sub: Version 3: one small child, and a better sibling replaces it

groups.note: A version 3 child may be 1,000 bytes at most; 1,350 fails.
A small child of 141 bytes is accepted without trouble.

rows: ev = ['sibling eviction' in r1, 'ok' in r2]
groups.note: A second child replaces the first only at a higher rate.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: limits of a version 3 family
The family stays small, and a better sibling can always replace a pinning one.

slides.notes: A version 3 parent may have one child of at most 1,000 virtual bytes. A child of 1,350 is refused and one of 141 is accepted. A second child at the same rate is refused, and one at a higher rate evicts its sibling, so a pin cannot last. The rules are called topologically restricted until confirmation, which is the long name of version 3 payments. It is example 22 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Strict limits make the worst case of pinning small and known

slides.title: Pay to anchor: a spendable output
slides.sub: A zero-fee parent with an output anyone can spend

Alone it is refused; with its child it is accepted.
The child spends the anchor with an empty witness.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: the anchor and the package
The anchor carries no value and needs no key: the child that spends it brings the fee.

slides.notes: The parent has a zero-value output with the script 51024e73, which anyone can spend, and it pays no fee. Alone the node refuses it. The child spends the anchor with an empty witness and pays 10,000 satoshis, so the package is accepted. This is the form that Lightning channels use to add the fee after the payment was signed. slides.title: A pre-signed payment cannot guess its fee
slides.sub: Matt Corallo's proposal, 29 November 2018

items.cap: Lightning Network logo - Ole Henrik Skogstrom, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: On Thursday 29 November 2018 Matt Corallo wrote to the bitcoin-dev and lightning-dev lists that pre-signed Lightning transactions cannot predict next week's fee.
A counterparty could chain a large, moderate-fee child to a commitment's spare output and pin it near the mempool's bottom.
Corallo's carve-out let one small extra child through; Bitcoin Core 0.19.0.1 shipped it in 2019 at 10,000 virtual bytes, not the book's 1,000.
Bitcoin Core 31.0 later removed the carve-out altogether when it adopted the cluster mempool.

items.body: Stand-in picture: the Lightning logo, not the proposal

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 29 November 2018. Matt Corallo wrote that Lightning channels exchange pre-signed transactions that are broadcast much later, so their fee has to be predicted or added afterwards by a child. The lesson is that a limit built for one attack can outlive the problem it solved. The picture is a stand-in; the link leads to the proposal on the mailing list.

slides.title: Fee sniping and incentives
slides.sub: Fee sniping is a miner re-mining a block to take its best fees.

items.meaning: A block pays a subsidy and the fees of its payments.
A miner may re-mine a block to take its best fees.
Wallets lock a payment to the next block height.

slides.notes: A block pays a subsidy and fees, and the mix changes. When fees dominate, a miner may gain by re-mining a block. This part computes the odds of winning such a race and shows how wallets defend with the lock time. The three examples of the part use the census of two real blocks and the recorded run of Bitcoin Core on a test network.

slides.title: Block 840,000: fees were nearly the reward
slides.sub: ViaBTC and block 840,000, 20 April 2024

items.cap: Bitcoin mining farm - Marko Ahtisaari, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: Block 840,000 was found on 20 April 2024 at 00:09 UTC by the pool ViaBTC, the first block after Bitcoin's fourth halving.
The halving cut the subsidy from 6.25 to 3.125 bitcoins, so fees made up nearly all of that block's reward.
Fees totalled 3,762,561,499 satoshis of a 4,075,061,499 reward, 92.33 percent, against just 0.46 percent in block 971,489.
The chapter's claim that the subsidy dwarfs the fees is true of the later block and false of this one.

items.body: Stand-in picture: a mining farm, not the pool ViaBTC

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 20 April 2024. Block 840,000 was found at 00:09 UTC by the pool ViaBTC and held 3,050 transactions. It was the first block after the fourth halving, and its fees were nearly the whole reward. The lesson is to check a book's claim against the block, because the market moves. The picture is a stand-in; the link leads to the block.

slides.title: Odds of winning a sniping race
slides.sub: How hash rate turns into the chance to re-mine a block

groups.note: The chance to win a re-mining race is (x/(1-x)) squared.

rows: pct = [round(100 * p, 2) for p in odds]
groups.note: At 45 percent two in three; at half the rate, certain.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: chance to win the re-mining race, percent
At 45 percent of the hash rate the chance is 66.94 percent; at half it is certain.

slides.notes: A miner with a share x of the hash rate wins the race to re-mine a block with probability x over one minus x, squared. That is 1.23 percent at 10 percent of the hash rate and 66.94 percent at 45 percent. At half the hash rate the chance is certain. The listing computes the formula with the chapter library for four shares. It is example 26 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: With 45 percent of the hash rate a miner wins two races in three

slides.title: What if nobody got a subsidy?
slides.sub: A Princeton paper, 21 October 2016

items.cap: Nassau Hall, Princeton University - Smallbones, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

items: On 21 October 2016 Arvind Narayanan announced on Princeton's CITP blog a paper on Bitcoin's instability without the block reward.
Narayanan, Miles Carlsten, Harry Kalodner and Matt Weinberg argued that once fees replace rewards a miner can gain by undercutting a rival's block.
Their model, and this chapter's run, puts a 45-percent miner's odds of re-mining a block ahead of a rival at 66.94 percent.
Wallets guard against this by locking a payment's spend to the chain's current height.

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 21 October 2016. Arvind Narayanan announced on the Princeton CITP blog the paper On the Instability of Bitcoin Without the Block Reward, written with Miles Carlsten, Harry Kalodner and Matt Weinberg and presented at ACM CCS the next week. When fees are the main income, a miner can gain by undercutting a rival's block. The link leads to the blog post.

A payment is not final in the block of its lock time.

A lock time at the tip keeps a payment out of any block that a sniper re-mines.

slides.notes: A wallet sets the lock time of a payment to the current height, so that a miner who rewrites the block cannot take it. Of 60 payments in the test, 56 sit at the tip and four are set back. Such a payment is not final in the block of that height. The result table also counts the payments of the two census blocks whose lock time is the tip. It is example 27 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A lock time equal to the tip makes a re-mined block useless to the sniper

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.sub: One line per group of parts, each provable from its slides

items: The fee is inputs minus outputs: no field holds it, and only the spender can change it.
Miners sort by fee rate in satoshis per virtual byte; the relay floor and dust set minimums.
A payment is replaced by a copy that pays the old fee plus its own size; full replacement is the default.
A child pays for its parent as one package; clusters, TRUC and anchors bound pinning.
When fees replace the subsidy, a miner may snipe a block, and wallets defend with the lock time.

slides.notes: These five lines are the deck in miniature. A line that feels unproven should send the reader back to its code slide, because every figure in it was computed there. The chapter code tab of the course page reruns all twenty-seven examples, so each line can be checked and changed by editing the listing. The five lines also answer the seven questions of the opening, grouped by part.
